StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language
Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning

Chi Yan Affiliation:  The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) Affiliation:  XPENG Robotics    Guoyang Zhao Affiliation:  XPENG Robotics    Wentao Yuan Affiliation:  XPENG Robotics    Yixiao Ge Affiliation:  XPENG Robotics    Yanning Zhou Affiliation:  XPENG Robotics    Dan Xu Email: {cyanao,danxu}@cse.ust.hk* Equal contribution.‡ Project leader.† Corresponding authors. Affiliation:  The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST)
Abstract

Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy (δ1\delta_{1}) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model’s performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

1 Introduction

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and reasoning about visual content in the digital world (Alayrac et al., 2022). Building upon these advances, recent efforts have begun to extend such capabilities beyond the digital realm into the physical world, positioning VLMs as a key foundation for embodied AI (Driess et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). However, extending VLMs from the digital to the physical world requires more than semantic understanding: it demands geometrically grounded spatial intelligence for reasoning and acting in 3D environments.

To extend VLMs beyond semantic understanding, recent studies have explored various ways to enhance their spatial reasoning capabilities. SpatialVLM (Chen et al., 2024) learns qualitative and quantitative spatial concepts from large-scale spatial question-answering data, while SpatialRGPT (Cheng et al., 2024) augments region-level representations with monocular depth cues for object-centric reasoning. 3D-LLM (Hong et al., 2023), in contrast, grounds language models in reconstructed 3D scene representations. Despite these advances, spatial benchmarks such as VSI-Bench reveal persistent limitations in current models’ ability to construct and reason about 3D space from visual observations (Yang et al., 2025). Moreover, the geometric information available to these models is typically inferred from monocular observations or supplied through estimated depth and reconstructed 3D representations, making it difficult to determine whether their spatial predictions are grounded in geometric evidence directly available from visual observations or primarily reflect learned priors—a concern reinforced by evidence-absent evaluations showing that VLMs can exploit scene- and category-level priors (Zhang et al., 2026).

Calibrated stereo provides explicit geometric constraints for metric 3D perception: cross-view correspondences determine disparity, which can be converted into metric depth using known camera intrinsics and baseline. Yet, providing binocular observations alone does not guarantee that a VLM will acquire geometric representations that generalize beyond the training distribution. Existing stereo methods primarily focus on geometric estimation, while VLMs typically treat paired images as generic visual inputs without explicitly learning the geometric relations between them. This raises a central question: How can a VLM learn transferable representations from binocular geometry that support metric 3D perception and high-level spatial reasoning? To investigate this question, we introduce StereoVLM, a geometry-aware binocular VLM designed to learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated stereo observations.

To connect binocular geometry with spatial understanding, we organize the training supervision into a hierarchy of tasks spanning pixel-level correspondence, disparity estimation, calibration-conditioned metric depth, and object-level spatial reasoning. This hierarchy progressively connects cross-view matching to image-space geometric measurement and then to metric-scale estimation, before extending the learned geometry to language-referred objects and task-relevant 3D grounding. Importantly, we find that disparity provides a substantially more generalizable supervision signal than direct binocular depth on unseen environments, motivating its role as an intermediate geometric representation between cross-view correspondence and metric depth. We further establish Stereo3D-Bench to evaluate this progression across point-level geometry, object-level geometry, and object-level spatial reasoning. Beyond conventional task accuracy, controlled right-view interventions and geometric out-of-distribution evaluation test whether model predictions genuinely depend on valid cross-view geometry. Compared with matched training without stereo instructions, hierarchical geometric supervision raises the five-benchmark spatial-reasoning average by 3.54 points and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) manipulation success by 4.3 percentage points.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning, with hierarchical supervision that connects cross-view correspondence and disparity to calibration-conditioned metric depth and language-grounded spatial reasoning, yielding transferable 3D spatial representations.

  • •

    We establish Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark spanning point-level geometry, object-level geometry, and object-level spatial reasoning, together with a verifiable evaluation protocol that uses controlled input interventions and geometric out-of-distribution evaluation to test whether predictions genuinely rely on binocular geometry.

  • •

    We demonstrate that disparity provides a more generalizable geometric supervision signal than direct binocular depth on unseen environments, while hierarchical geometric supervision benefits broader spatial reasoning and downstream embodied control.

2 Related Work

Spatial reasoning in vision-language models

Existing studies have enhanced spatial reasoning in VLMs through spatial instruction tuning (Chen et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2026), depth-aware visual representations (Cheng et al., 2024), and 3D grounding (Hong et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b). Meanwhile, benchmarks such as VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025) reveal that current multimodal models still struggle with metric 3D understanding and spatial reasoning. Recent works explore metric depth prediction in VLMs, including queried-point prediction in DepthLM (Yeh et al., 2026) and dense prediction in DepthVLM (Yu et al., 2026). VLM3 (Cai et al., 2026) covers metric depth, cross-image correspondence, camera pose estimation, and object-level 3D understanding through separate task-specific training. Joint learning across low-level geometry and high-level semantic spatial understanding remains less explored.

Stereo vision and embodied intelligence

Stereo vision recovers scene geometry by establishing cross-view correspondence and converting disparity into depth using camera calibration. Modern stereo methods, including RAFT-Stereo (Lipson et al., 2021), IGEV-Stereo (Xu et al., 2023), FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) and S2M2 (Min et al., 2025), employ correlation or geometry volumes to achieve accurate and generalizable disparity estimation. Recent work has begun incorporating binocular sensing into embodied systems. StereoVLA (Deng et al., 2025) fuses stereo-geometric and monocular-semantic features and adds auxiliary depth and camera-parameter objectives for VLA manipulation, while StereoPolicy (Han et al., 2026) uses cross-view attention to adapt diffusion policies and pretrained VLA policies without explicit 3D reconstruction. EATR-Stereo (Wu et al., 2026) further routes paired-view evidence according to proprioceptive state for long-horizon humanoid control, and VLBiMan (Zhou and Jia, 2026) combines vision-language grounding with calibrated stereo reconstruction in a modular one-shot bimanual system. These methods demonstrate the value of binocular cues, with a primary focus on geometric estimation or embodied action. Our work bridges embodied stereo sensing and VLM spatial reasoning through a stereo VLM jointly trained on cross-view correspondence, disparity estimation, calibration-conditioned metric depth perception, and high-level semantic spatial reasoning.

3 Stereo3D-Bench

Stereo3D-Bench evaluates whether binocular evidence supporting metric geometry also transfers to language-grounded understanding of objects and task-relevant 3D structure. Its main split draws on four data sources—DROID, Xperience-10M, FSD, and RoboCasa—and covers all eight tasks. An out-of-domain (OOD) split uses independently collected in-house data to evaluate point-level correspondence, disparity, and depth. Figure 2 illustrates the benchmark construction and task hierarchy. Controlled right-view interventions further test whether predictions depend on valid cross-view correspondence rather than merely on the presence of a second image. The supplementary material details data and question construction (appendix A), split and leakage controls (appendix B), and the evaluation protocol (appendix C).

3.1 Task Hierarchy

Stereo3D-Bench comprises eight tasks across three levels: three point-level geometry tasks, three object-level geometry tasks, and two object-level spatial reasoning tasks. Each query is posed as a short language question on an ordered stereo pair. Depending on the task, the model returns a coordinate, a scalar, a 2D box, or an oriented 3D box with an object label.

Point-level geometry. Given a queried pixel in the left image, the model predicts its corresponding location in the right image, its horizontal disparity, or its metric depth along the left-camera optical axis. These tasks assess the model’s ability to establish cross-view correspondence, estimate binocular disparity, and recover metric scene geometry from stereo observations.

Object-level geometry. The same three geometric tasks are applied to an object specified by language. Object correspondence returns its matching bounding box in the right image, object disparity predicts its representative disparity, and object depth predicts its representative metric depth along the left-camera optical axis.

Object-level spatial reasoning. Oriented 3D grounding identifies a referred object and predicts its label and oriented 3D bounding box in the rectified-left camera frame. Task-target grounding instead receives a manipulation instruction, identifies the object to be manipulated, and predicts that object’s oriented 3D bounding box.

Together, these tasks test whether a model can progress from matching individual pixels, to associating geometry with named objects, and to grounding task-relevant objects in metric 3D space.

3.2 Data Sources and VQA Construction

The main split combines real-world data from DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) and Xperience-10M (Ropedia, 2026) with synthetic data from FSD (Wen et al., 2025) and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024). For the synthetic sources, FSD provides rendered ground-truth disparity, while RoboCasa provides ground-truth disparity and depth directly from the simulator. FSD lacks physical metric calibration and is therefore evaluated only for correspondence and disparity.

For the real-world sources, DROID provides aligned sensor depth, while Xperience-10M provides its officially released metric stereo-depth annotations. The five object-level tasks are evaluated on DROID and Xperience-10M.

Evaluation data.

The main split uses held-out samples from the four sources above. Training and evaluation data are separated before annotation generation. DROID is split by scene (laboratory, robot, and collection date), and Xperience-10M by recording UUID; all images and derived questions from held-out groups are excluded from training. FSD evaluation frames are excluded from training, while RoboCasa reserves five of its 24 task identities for evaluation and excludes all associated samples from training. To further assess geometric generalization to unseen scenes, we independently collected an in-house OOD test set covering point-level correspondence, disparity, and depth. Results are reported separately. Split details are provided in appendix B.

VQA construction.

Using the source-specific geometric references described above, we construct question-answer pairs for the tasks in section 3.1. Point-level queries are sampled from valid image regions. For real-world sources, S2M2 (Min et al., 2025) provides an independent consistency check. A pixel 𝐩l\mathbf{p}_{l} is eligible only when both depth values are valid and satisfy

|ZS2M2​(𝐩l)−Znative​(𝐩l)|Znative​(𝐩l)≤0.10,\frac{\left|Z_{\mathrm{S2M2}}(\mathbf{p}_{l})-Z_{\mathrm{native}}(\mathbf{p}_{l})\right|}{Z_{\mathrm{native}}(\mathbf{p}_{l})}\leq 0.10, (1)

where ZS2M2Z_{\mathrm{S2M2}} is the depth recovered from S2M2 disparity using camera calibration and ZnativeZ_{\mathrm{native}} is the source-native depth reference. Further spatial filtering is detailed in section A.2. S2M2 is used only for filtering; numerical answers are derived from the source-native references. For each stereo pair and applicable point-level task, we sample 120 points and group them into 15 questions of eight points each. QA counts refer to grouped questions rather than individual points.

For object-level queries, Qwen3 (Bai et al., 2025) proposes objects, SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026) generates their masks, and DAM (Lian et al., 2025) provides region descriptions to reject semantically inconsistent proposals. For each retained object ii, we back-project its valid pixels into a point cloud in the rectified-left camera frame:

𝒫i={Znative​(𝐩)​𝐊l−1​𝐩~|𝐩∈ℳi∩𝒱},\mathcal{P}_{i}=\left\{Z_{\mathrm{native}}(\mathbf{p})\,\mathbf{K}_{l}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{p}}\;\middle|\;\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{M}_{i}\cap\mathcal{V}\right\}, (2)

where ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i} is the object’s segmentation mask, 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the valid pixel set after all filtering steps, 𝐊l\mathbf{K}_{l} is the left-camera intrinsic matrix, and 𝐩~=(u,v,1)⊤\tilde{\mathbf{p}}=(u,v,1)^{\top} is the homogeneous pixel coordinate. We estimate object extent and orientation in a gravity-aligned frame obtained from DROID camera extrinsics or estimated for Xperience-10M, then transform the boxes back to the rectified-left camera frame. Task-specific templates convert the annotations into questions and structured answers, with camera calibration included in metric-depth queries. Both training and benchmark annotations undergo automatic semantic filtering and box–mask reprojection checks; benchmark questions additionally receive manual review.

Training follows the same question schemas but uses FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) for numerical supervision. Where source-native references are available, their agreement with FoundationStereo identifies reliable training regions. FoundationStereo is used neither to filter benchmark pixels nor to generate benchmark answers. Details are provided in appendix A.

3.3 Binocular Controls

A correct prediction does not by itself demonstrate that the model uses binocular evidence. We evaluate each query under five input conditions while holding the checkpoint, question, calibration, and decoding procedure fixed. Correct stereo (𝐈l,𝐈r)(\mathbf{I}_{l},\mathbf{I}_{r}) defines the primary benchmark score; the other four conditions are diagnostic controls. Single left supplies only 𝐈l\mathbf{I}_{l}, whereas zero right supplies (𝐈l,𝟎)(\mathbf{I}_{l},\mathbf{0}), where 𝟎\mathbf{0} is a zero-valued image with the same dimensions as 𝐈r\mathbf{I}_{r}. These controls test whether any improvement requires visual evidence from the right image rather than merely a second image slot. Duplicated left supplies (𝐈l,𝐈l)(\mathbf{I}_{l},\mathbf{I}_{l}), removing the binocular displacement while preserving the same scene content. Shuffled right supplies (𝐈l,𝐈r′)(\mathbf{I}_{l},\mathbf{I}^{\prime}_{r}), where 𝐈r′\mathbf{I}^{\prime}_{r} is taken from another benchmark sample. It preserves a natural second image but breaks the cross-view correspondence. Together, these controls test whether predictions depend on the geometrically matching right view.

4 StereoVLM

StereoVLM adapts a pretrained vision-language model to binocular spatial reasoning through hierarchical instruction supervision. We first formulate the model inputs and outputs, then describe how stereo geometry connects the supervision targets, and finally introduce the joint training strategy. Figure 3 summarizes the architecture and training pipeline.

4.1 Model Formulation

Given an ordered pair of rectified stereo images (Il,Ir)(I_{l},I_{r}) and a question qq, StereoVLM generates a textual answer aa describing the queried geometric or spatial property:

pθ​(a∣Il,Ir,q)=∏t=1Tpθ​(at∣Il,Ir,q,a<t),\vskip-2.0ptp_{\theta}(a\mid I_{l},I_{r},q)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid I_{l},I_{r},q,a_{<t}),\vskip-2.0pt (3)

where θ\theta denotes the model parameters, TT is the answer length, and ata_{t} and a<ta_{<t} denote the current and preceding answer tokens, respectively. The question specifies image points, a referred object, or a manipulation instruction, and includes camera calibration, including the horizontal focal length fxf_{x} and stereo baseline BB, when metric geometry is required. These parameters allow predictions to account for the physical scale of the stereo setup. Built on Qwen3-VL-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), StereoVLM processes both images and the textual query through the pretrained vision-language architecture. We adapt this model using hierarchical geometric supervision, as described below.

4.2 Hierarchical Geometric Supervision

From correspondence to metric depth.

We formulate point-level supervision as three complementary predictions of the same underlying stereo geometry: correspondence, disparity, and metric depth. Their targets are derived from a shared FoundationStereo disparity estimate (section A.2), with camera calibration providing the conversion to metric scale. For a queried pixel 𝐩l=(ul,vl)\mathbf{p}_{l}=(u_{l},v_{l}) in IlI_{l}, its correspondence 𝐩r=(ur,vr)\mathbf{p}_{r}=(u_{r},v_{r}) in IrI_{r} satisfies vl≃vrv_{l}\simeq v_{r}, and

d⁡(𝐩l)=ul−ur.\vskip-2.0ptd(\mathbf{p}_{l})=u_{l}-u_{r}.\vskip-2.0pt (4)

When physical calibration is available, the depth target along the left-camera optical axis is given by

Z⁡(𝐩l)=fx​Bd⁡(𝐩l),d⁡(𝐩l)>0.\vskip-2.0ptZ(\mathbf{p}_{l})=\frac{f_{x}B}{d(\mathbf{p}_{l})},\qquad d(\mathbf{p}_{l})>0.\vskip-2.0pt (5)

Here, disparity dd and focal length fxf_{x} are in pixels, while baseline BB and depth ZZ are in meters.

We encode these targets as separate question-answer pairs and jointly optimize the model across all three question types. Correspondence supervision emphasizes cross-view localization, disparity supervision quantifies image-space displacement, and depth supervision requires interpreting that displacement under the supplied calibration. Deriving all three targets from a common geometric reference preserves their geometric relationship during target construction, while joint training encourages the model to learn both cross-view matching and its connection to metric scale.

Language-grounded object supervision.

Point-level supervision captures local stereo geometry. To associate this geometry with semantic entities and their spatial extent, we introduce object-level supervision conditioned on linguistic references. Object correspondence, disparity, and depth link the referred object to its cross-view location and geometric measurements, while oriented 3D grounding supervises its position, dimensions, and orientation in the rectified-left camera frame. Task-target grounding further requires the model to identify and localize the object specified by a manipulation instruction. Together, these objectives extend supervision from local geometric estimation to language-conditioned object localization and task-relevant 3D grounding.

4.3 Joint Training Objective

We jointly optimize StereoVLM over point-level geometry, object-level grounding, and general multimodal instructions. All tasks share the conditional answer-generation formulation in section 4.1, allowing geometric measurements and language-grounded spatial outputs to be learned under a unified objective. Let 𝒟mix\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mix}} denote the resulting instruction distribution and xx the visual and textual input, with x=(Il,Ir,q)x=(I_{l},I_{r},q) for stereo examples. The training objective is

ℒSFT​(θ)=−𝔼(x,a)∼𝒟mix​[∑t=1Tlog⁡pθ​(at∣x,a<t)].\vskip-2.0pt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,a)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{mix}}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid x,a_{<t})\right]. (6)

The loss is applied only to answer tokens. Point- and object-level instructions are interleaved throughout training, so the supervision hierarchy describes complementary levels of spatial understanding rather than sequential optimization stages. Details are reported in section 5.1.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Model and training setup.

We initialize StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B from the corresponding Qwen3-VL-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) checkpoints. Unless otherwise specified, our final models are instruction-tuned for 3,000 steps with all parameters updated, using an initial learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, a warmup ratio of 0.030.03, and an effective global batch size of 64. Stereo images are processed at a resolution of 800×320800\times 320. Stereo instructions account for 25% of the sampled training mixture, with 15% assigned to point-level geometry and 10% to object-level supervision. The remaining 75% comprises general visual-language, grounding, spatial-reasoning, tracking, and robotics instructions. Full data and optimization details are provided in section D.1.

Evaluation.

We evaluate StereoVLM on Stereo3D-Bench for binocular geometry and object-level spatial understanding, on five external benchmarks (Omni3D (Brazil et al., 2023), DA-2K (Yang et al., 2024), OmniSpatial (Jia et al., 2026), MindCube (Wang et al., 2025a), and VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025)) for spatial-reasoning transfer, and on RoboCasa for manipulation performance. We further assess geometric generalization on the independently collected in-house OOD split of Stereo3D-Bench, focusing on point-level correspondence, disparity, and depth. Evaluation splits are described in appendix B. Settings specific to each experiment are provided in the corresponding subsections.

5.2 Learning Transferable Binocular Representations

We analyze how the choice of geometric supervision affects metric-depth generalization. We compare monocular depth, binocular depth, and binocular disparity under a controlled geometry-only setting. We then analyze whether joint disparity–depth training learns the calibrated conversion between the two quantities and whether geometric supervision benefits object-level spatial understanding.

Which geometric supervision generalizes better?

We initialize all three variants from the same Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct checkpoint and train them exclusively on geometry QA constructed from the same 234K rectified stereo pairs, using an identical optimization budget. The monocular-depth variant receives only the left image and directly predicts metric depth. The binocular-depth variant receives the ordered stereo pair and camera calibration and also predicts depth directly. The binocular-disparity variant predicts horizontal disparity from the ordered pair; at evaluation, depth is recovered using calibration via eq. 5.

Table 1 shows that the benefit of binocular input depends on the supervision target. Compared with monocular supervision, direct binocular depth supervision increases δ1\delta_{1} from 77.91% to 87.26% on the main split, but decreases it from 51.00% to 45.89% on the OOD split. In contrast, binocular disparity supervision achieves the best results across all three depth metrics on both splits. On the OOD split, it reaches a δ1\delta_{1} of 74.92%, outperforming direct binocular depth supervision by 29.03 percentage points. These results suggest that binocular input alone is insufficient for reliable generalization and support disparity as an intermediate representation for metric depth estimation across unseen scenes.

Consistency of direct and disparity-derived depth.

We next examine whether joint disparity–depth supervision connects the two output spaces. For each jointly trained model, we compare two depth estimates at the same query points: directly predicted metric depth and depth recovered from predicted disparity via the calibrated conversion in eq. 5.

Table 3 shows that both routes achieve similar MAE and δ1\delta_{1} at both model scales. The δ1\delta_{1} gaps are only 0.05 and 0.02 percentage points for StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B, respectively, with corresponding MAE differences of 0.05 cm and 0.17 cm. Direct prediction performs slightly better across all reported metrics, with a more pronounced difference in 8B RMSE (29.93 vs. 32.63 cm). Overall, these results support the link between disparity and calibrated depth under joint supervision while preserving accurate direct prediction.

Does geometry supervision improve object-level performance?

We compare the full StereoVLM-2B model in Table 4 with a variant trained without point-level geometry QA supervision. Table 3 shows that this supervision improves all five object-level metrics. The largest gains occur in object disparity Acc@2px and 3D-box mIoU, with improvements of 21.59 and 9.82 percentage points. Correspondence mIoU, object depth δ1\delta_{1}, and target Joint@0.25 also improve by 2.67, 5.87, and 2.57 points. These results indicate that supervision on local stereo geometry benefits language-grounded object-level reasoning, particularly the estimation of cross-view displacement and 3D extent.

5.3 Main Results

We compare StereoVLM with general-purpose multi-image VLMs and monocular depth-specialized VLMs on Stereo3D-Bench, with results reported in Table 4. StereoVLM and the multi-image baselines receive the same ordered stereo pair, whereas monocular depth models receive only the rectified left image. We follow each baseline’s official preprocessing and inference settings, including its model-specific input resolution. Before scoring, predicted image coordinates and disparities expressed on the width-1000 normalized scale are converted to pixels at the benchmark image resolution. Results are reported only for tasks supported by each model.

Point-level geometry.

StereoVLM-8B achieves the best results across all three point-level tasks in Table 4. Under the same stereo-input protocol, it reduces correspondence MAE from 9.27 to 3.80 pixels and disparity MAE from 7.55 to 3.76 pixels relative to GPT-6 Astra, while increasing depth δ1\delta_{1} from 75.96% to 95.17%. StereoVLM-2B also surpasses GPT-6 Astra on all three tasks, reaching 94.51% in depth δ1\delta_{1}. The remaining general-purpose VLMs exhibit substantially weaker stereo geometric performance, whereas the depth-specialized baselines receive only the left image and do not exploit binocular evidence in this evaluation. Compared with the single-view DepthVLM-4B reference, StereoVLM-8B improves depth δ1\delta_{1} by 58.06 percentage points. Together, these results show consistent improvements in image-space geometry and metric-depth estimation across both model scales.

Language-grounded 3D reasoning.

Across the five object-level tasks, StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B achieve average scores of 64.43% and 66.98%, outperforming GPT-6 Astra by 16.82 and 19.37 percentage points, respectively. The advantage is particularly pronounced in 3D localization: StereoVLM-8B increases oriented 3D-box mIoU from 17.92% to 37.70% and target Joint@0.25 from 12.82% to 51.28%. Both variants also surpass the single-view DepthVLM-4B reference, which achieves an object-level average of 14.35%. Scaling from 2B to 8B improves all five object-level metrics. These results demonstrate stronger 3D grounding of language-referred objects and task targets, complementing the gains in point-level geometry. We also outperform cascaded pipelines in accuracy and efficiency (section D.8).

Depth visualization.

As shown in fig. 4, we qualitatively compare StereoVLM-2B with existing depth-specialized VLMs on representative samples from Stereo3D-Bench. StereoVLM-2B produces the most faithful depth reconstructions among the compared methods, recovering the overall scene geometry while better preserving object boundaries and foreground structure. Notably, StereoVLM-2B achieves these results with substantially fewer parameters than the two baselines: approximately half as many as DepthVLM-4B and one-sixth as many as DepthLM-13B.

Binocular evidence and single-view capability.

To assess whether StereoVLM’s gains depend on valid binocular evidence, we evaluate StereoVLM-2B under the five input conditions in Table 5. Only the right-view input changes; the checkpoint, left image, query, calibration, and decoding settings remain fixed. Note that the single-left control retains stereo calibration, whereas the single-view protocol in Appendix D.3 also removes the baseline information. Correct stereo achieves the best results across all reported metrics: relative to single-left input, disparity MAE decreases from 9.07 to 4.12 pixels, depth δ1\delta_{1} increases from 80.82% to 94.51%, and the object-level average rises from 40.26% to 64.43%. Zero-right performs similarly to single-left, indicating that retaining a second image slot without right-view content does not recover the stereo gain. Duplicated-left and shuffled-right both perform worse than single-left across all reported metrics, with duplicated-left producing the largest degradation. This shows that an invalid second view can impair prediction, rather than simply remove the benefit of stereo input. Together, these controls support the importance of correctly paired right-view evidence for geometric and object-level accuracy, while the single-left results show retained single-view capability. Baseline perturbations further support the model’s use of the supplied baseline for depth prediction (section D.5).

5.4 Transfer Beyond Stereo3D-Bench

We test spatial reasoning and embodied control using matched 2B models trained with and without stereo instructions. Both share the same initialization, optimization schedule, and training budget. Removing stereo instructions preserves the relative sampling proportions of the remaining categories.

General spatial reasoning.

We evaluate general spatial reasoning on three monocular benchmarks (Omni3D, DA-2K, and OmniSpatial) and two video benchmarks (MindCube and VSI-Bench). Table 7 shows that adding stereo instructions improves all five benchmarks, increasing the overall average from 47.94 to 51.48, a gain of 3.54 percentage points. The largest gain occurs on Omni3D at 8.21 points, while the video benchmarks MindCube and VSI-Bench improve by 3.71 and 0.92 points, respectively. With shared spatial supervision, correct stereo and single-left training yield similar averages (50.23 and 50.21). Adding correspondence and disparity supervision to correct stereo raises the average to 51.48 (section D.6.1).

Embodied control.

We further evaluate whether the learned representation benefits downstream robotic control. We initialize the same GR00T policy (Bjorck et al., 2025) architecture from the pretrained Qwen3-VL-2B model and representation models trained with and without stereo instructions. Each policy is trained for 60k steps using 50 demonstrations per task and evaluated on 24 RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) tasks with 50 rollouts per task. To isolate the benefit of stereo supervision from exposure to RoboCasa data during representation training, we exclude RoboCasa from the representation-training mixture for this embodied-control experiment.

Table 7 shows that stereo instruction tuning increases manipulation success from 38.1% to 42.4%, a gain of 4.3 percentage points over general instruction tuning alone. It also exceeds the pretrained Qwen3-VL-2B initialization at 34.9% by 7.5 points. All policies share the same stereo-input setting and downstream training protocol. Further controls support the benefits of geometric supervision and valid binocular observations for manipulation (section D.6.2).

6 Conclusion and Limitations

We present StereoVLM, a geometry-aware binocular vision-language model for metric 3D spatial reasoning, trained with hierarchical stereo supervision from cross-view correspondence and disparity to calibration-conditioned metric depth and semantic spatial reasoning. We show that disparity supervision provides substantially stronger metric-depth generalization to unseen environments than direct binocular depth supervision, while controlled interventions verify that StereoVLM benefits from valid cross-view geometry. Hierarchical geometric supervision further benefits broader spatial reasoning and downstream embodied control. The current study is limited by its focus on controlled benchmarks and simulated kitchen tasks, as well as its reliance on calibrated and synchronized cameras; future work should address the simulation-to-real gap and improve robustness to challenging visual conditions and diverse robot platforms.

Supplementary Material

This supplementary material documents the construction and evaluation of Stereo3D-Bench, together with additional training details and experiments for StereoVLM. Training and benchmark pairs follow a shared processing and annotation procedure but are kept separate by the data split. The sections below describe this procedure, the split, the evaluation protocol, and supporting results.
⊳\triangleright appendix A: Geometric references, semantic annotations, and query and answer schemas, with point-level and object-level examples.
⊳\triangleright appendix B: The training mixture, the main and OOD splits of Stereo3D-Bench, and per-source counts for the main split.
⊳\triangleright appendix C: Metric definitions, invalid outputs, and the implementation of right-view interventions.
⊳\triangleright appendix D: Training settings, geometric generalization, input controls, extrinsic robustness, baseline sensitivity, transfer experiments, and modular stereo–VLM comparisons.

Appendix A Data Construction

Training data and Stereo3D-Bench share the same stereo representation, question schemas, and coordinate conventions, but intentionally use different geometric-reference pathways. Training supervision uses FoundationStereo predictions, whereas Stereo3D-Bench is scored against source-native geometric references. This separation prevents benchmark performance from directly measuring reproduction of the stereo estimator used to construct the training data. The following subsections describe the shared representation, the training and evaluation reference pathways, the semantic annotations, and question generation. Dataset splitting and leakage control are described in appendix B.

A.1 Unified Stereo Data Representation

Every source sample is converted into an ordered, rectified stereo pair at a resolution of 800×320800\times 320. During preprocessing, camera intrinsics are standardized across calibrated stereo datasets. We retain the rectified camera metadata, including the horizontal focal length fxf_{x}, stereo baseline BB, and camera extrinsics when provided by the source. Disparity is expressed in rectified-left pixel coordinates, and physical depth is represented by the left-camera optical-axis distance in meters.

Training and evaluation pairs use the same representation but differ in reference provenance. FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) provides dense disparity supervision for the training mixture. In Stereo3D-Bench, DROID uses its aligned sensor depth, Xperience-10M uses its officially released stereo-depth annotation, RoboCasa uses simulator geometry, and FSD uses its source-native disparity reference. Because FSD does not provide physical metric calibration, it contributes correspondence and disparity questions but not metric-depth questions. Figure 5 compares the source-native references with the outputs of S2M2 and FoundationStereo.

A.2 Point-Level Geometric References

Training references.

For training samples with source-native geometric references, we retain pixels whose native reference is valid and agrees with FoundationStereo. FoundationStereo then provides the numerical disparity target on these filtered regions. When physical calibration is available, disparity is converted to metric depth as

Z=fx​Bd.Z=\frac{f_{x}B}{d}. (7)

Thus, the training target is provided by FoundationStereo, while source-native references are used to identify reliable training regions.

Benchmark references.

Stereo3D-Bench uses source-native geometry rather than FoundationStereo outputs. For DROID, the numerical depth target is the aligned ZED sensor depth. For Xperience-10M, it is the officially released metric stereo-depth annotation. For RoboCasa, depth and disparity are obtained directly from the simulator. FSD supplies source-native disparity but no physical metric-depth reference and is therefore excluded from metric-depth evaluation. When a physical depth reference ZZ is available, its disparity and right-image correspondence are derived using

d=fx​BZ,xr=xl−d.d=\frac{f_{x}B}{Z},\qquad x^{r}=x^{l}-d. (8)

For the two real-image sources, DROID and Xperience-10M, we use S2M2 (Min et al., 2025), a separately trained stereo estimator that is not used to generate our training targets, as a reliability estimator. After converting its disparity to depth using the same physical calibration, a pixel is retained when both depths are valid and

|ZS2M2−Znative|Znative≤0.10.\frac{\left|Z_{\mathrm{S2M2}}-Z_{\mathrm{native}}\right|}{Z_{\mathrm{native}}}\leq 0.10. (9)

S2M2 determines only the validity mask; all benchmark answers are still computed from the source-native reference. Importantly, FoundationStereo, which supplies the training supervision, is not used to select benchmark pixels or to define their answers.

We additionally remove pixels within 16 pixels of the image boundary and pixels whose projected right-image locations fall outside the common valid crop. Local neighborhood checks suppress isolated valid pixels and discontinuities unsupported by neighboring reference values. These checks are applied before any evaluated model is run, and sampling uses a fixed random seed.

Point sampling.

Retained pixels are divided into a disparity-edge band and the remaining valid region. The edge band contains retained pixels within three pixels of a ridge in the source-native disparity map, ensuring that the candidate pool includes geometric boundaries rather than only large smooth surfaces. In the fixed Stereo3D-Bench protocol, each evaluated family contains 120 sampled points per pair, grouped into 15 questions of eight points each. Correspondence, disparity, and depth use separately sampled points but the same source-native reference and coordinate convention.

Figure 6 visualizes the reliability masks. The FoundationStereo agreement mask is included only as a diagnostic comparison with the training teacher; it is not used to construct Stereo3D-Bench.

A.3 Object-Level Semantic References

Object references are built from the rectified left image. Qwen3 (Bai et al., 2025) proposes object names, SAM3 (Carion et al., 2026) produces their masks, and DAM (Lian et al., 2025) supplies region descriptions used to reject semantically inconsistent proposals. The right image is not segmented. For benchmark pairs, object disparity, depth, right-image location, and lifted 3D geometry use the native references in section A.2, rather than FoundationStereo estimates.

Valid object pixels are lifted into the left-camera point cloud and expressed in a gravity-aligned frame, where object extent and yaw are estimated. The resulting oriented 3D box is then transformed back to the rectified-left camera frame. DROID reaches the gravity-aligned frame using the provided camera extrinsics. For the egocentric Xperience-10M images, the gravity-aligned frame is estimated because the camera optical axis is not generally perpendicular to the ground.

These references instantiate the five object-level tasks defined in section 3.1: object correspondence, object disparity, object depth, oriented 3D grounding, and task-target grounding. See fig. 7.

A.4 Question Generation and Quality Control

A question is formed from the references above and is posed on the ordered stereo pair. A point-level question lists one or more pixels in the left image, and the answer returns one value per pixel in the same order. Correspondence is a right-image coordinate, disparity is expressed on a normalized scale whose image width is 1000, and depth is in meters. The focal length and baseline are written into depth questions. An object-level question refers to an object by language. It asks for the object’s right-image box, its disparity, its depth, its oriented 3D box in the left-camera frame, or the label and 3D box of the object to manipulate.

Both training and Stereo3D-Bench apply the same automatic filters. Part of the proposed object list is removed. A 3D box is kept only when the box projected back onto the image has sufficient overlap with the object mask. Stereo3D-Bench then receives a manual review, and questions that remain low quality are removed. Training questions do not receive this review.

A.5 Question and Answer Schemas

We generate questions from task-specific templates. Each task has a fixed answer schema and multiple question paraphrases: two each for point correspondence, disparity, and depth; three each for object correspondence, disparity, and depth; five for oriented 3D grounding; and three for task-target grounding. Table 8 shows one paraphrase per task. Placeholders are replaced with the sample’s coordinates, object reference, instruction, and calibration.

Point queries list one or more pixels in the left image. For multiple pixels, the answer contains one numbered line per pixel in the same order; a single-pixel query returns only the requested value. Disparities are reported in width-normalized coordinates, d1000=1000​dpx/Wd_{1000}=1000d_{\mathrm{px}}/W, where WW is the image width in pixels. Depth is the left-camera zz coordinate in meters. Metric-depth questions state the rectified focal length and stereo baseline.

Object correspondence returns a right-image box [x1,y1,x2,y2][x_{1},y_{1},x_{2},y_{2}]. Object disparity and depth return a single numeric value in the same units as their point-level counterparts. Oriented 3D grounding and task-target grounding return an object label and a 3D box expressed in the left-camera frame.

Appendix B Splits and Leakage Control

Training data and Stereo3D-Bench follow the data-construction procedure in appendix A, while their source data are separated before stereo pairs, geometric references, semantic annotations, or questions are generated. Consequently, no benchmark image or question derived from it is used during training. Table 9 summarizes the resulting main-split composition.

For DROID, splitting is performed at the scene level. We define a scene by the laboratory, robot, and collection date. All recordings, episodes, camera views, and frames associated with one scene are assigned to the same split. For Xperience-10M, the recording UUID is used as the scene-grouping unit, and all episodes and frames from one recording remain together. Therefore, benchmark scenes from either source contribute neither images nor derived questions to training.

The remaining sources use source-specific exclusion units. FSD benchmark images are excluded from training at the source-frame level. RoboCasa contains 24 official task identities, five of which are reserved for evaluation. Samples from these five tasks are excluded from the training mixture, making the corresponding evaluation split disjoint at the task-identity level. FSD supplies correspondence and disparity references but no physical metric-depth reference; metric depth is therefore evaluated on the other 1,517 geometry pairs. The primary semantic benchmark excludes RoboCasa.

The OOD split of Stereo3D-Bench uses an independently collected in-house dataset and covers only point-level correspondence, disparity, and depth, with the same task definitions and metrics as the main split. Results are reported separately in table 11; table 9 counts only main-split samples.

In the fixed Stereo3D-Bench geometry protocol, each evaluated family uses 15 grouped questions per pair. DROID, Xperience-10M, and RoboCasa contain three geometry families, whereas FSD contains correspondence and disparity only. The geometry QA counts in table 9 refer to the standard stereo input and do not count repeated evaluations under right-view interventions.

Appendix C Evaluation Protocol

Point-level geometry.

Coordinates and disparities expressed on the width-1000 normalized scale are converted to pixels at the displayed image resolution before scoring. In particular, dpx=W​d1000/1000d_{\mathrm{px}}=Wd_{1000}/1000 for image width WW. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} contain all queried points for a task, and let 𝒫valid\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}} contain those with a successfully parsed, finite prediction. The primary correspondence error is the horizontal error of the disparity implied by the predicted right-image coordinate:

MAEcorr=1|𝒫valid|​∑i∈𝒫valid|(xil−x^ir)−di|.\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{corr}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}}\left|(x_{i}^{l}-\hat{x}_{i}^{r})-d_{i}\right|. (10)

Here xilx_{i}^{l} is the queried left-image coordinate, x^ir\hat{x}_{i}^{r} is the predicted right-image coordinate, and did_{i} is the reference disparity, all in pixels. The two-dimensional endpoint error and vertical coordinate error are retained as diagnostic metrics but do not enter the primary correspondence score. Disparity MAE is

MAEd=1|𝒫valid|​∑i∈𝒫valid|d^i−di|,\mathrm{MAE}_{d}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}}|\hat{d}_{i}-d_{i}|, (11)

also in pixels. The valid-point set is determined separately for each task; therefore, the correspondence and disparity denominators need not match.

For metric depth, we report MAE in centimeters, AbsRel, and δ1\delta_{1}:

MAEZ\displaystyle\mathrm{MAE}_{Z} =1|𝒫valid|​∑i∈𝒫valid|Z^i−Zi|,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}}|\hat{Z}_{i}-Z_{i}|, (12)
AbsRel\displaystyle\mathrm{AbsRel} =1|𝒫valid|​∑i∈𝒫valid|Z^i−Zi|Zi,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}}\frac{|\hat{Z}_{i}-Z_{i}|}{Z_{i}}, (13)
δ1\displaystyle\delta_{1} =1|𝒫|∑i∈𝒫valid[max(Z^iZi,ZiZ^i)<1.25].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{valid}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\max\!\left(\frac{\hat{Z}_{i}}{Z_{i}},\frac{Z_{i}}{\hat{Z}_{i}}\right)<1.25\right]. (14)

A valid depth prediction must additionally be positive. AbsRel is multiplied by 100 when reported as a percentage. MAE and AbsRel are computed over valid predictions, whereas the δ1\delta_{1} denominator contains all queried points; invalid depth predictions therefore count as failures under δ1\delta_{1}. Point-level metrics weight queried points equally rather than first averaging within each question.

Object-level semantics.

Object correspondence is measured by the IoU between the predicted and reference right-image boxes, averaged over all correspondence questions. An invalid box contributes an IoU of zero. Object disparity uses Acc​@​2​px\mathrm{Acc}@2\mathrm{px}, the fraction of questions satisfying |d^−d|≤2|\hat{d}-d|\leq 2 pixels after conversion from the width-1000 normalized scale. Object depth uses the δ1\delta_{1} definition above. Oriented 3D grounding uses the volumetric IoU between the predicted and reference oriented boxes in the rectified-left camera frame, averaged over all questions, with invalid boxes assigned zero IoU. Task-target grounding is correct only when the predicted target label is correct and its oriented 3D-box IoU is at least 0.250.25. The semantic average is the unweighted mean of these five task scores after each is expressed as a percentage.

Invalid outputs.

A prediction is invalid if it is missing, cannot be parsed into the required answer schema, contains non-finite values, gives a non-positive depth, or specifies an invalid 3D box. For a multi-point answer, parsed entries are scored individually and missing entries are marked invalid; entries beyond the requested number are ignored. Invalid semantic predictions receive zero IoU or count as failures for Acc​@​2​px\mathrm{Acc}@2\mathrm{px}, δ1\delta_{1}, and task-target grounding. Invalid point-level predictions are excluded from MAE and AbsRel but remain in the coverage denominator; invalid depth predictions also remain in the δ1\delta_{1} denominator.

Controlled right-view inputs.

For each query, the checkpoint, left image, question, calibration, and decoding configuration are held fixed. Correct stereo (Il,Ir)(I_{l},I_{r}) provides the primary benchmark score. Four diagnostic conditions alter the availability or validity of the right view. Single-left input removes the second image, (Il)(I_{l}). Duplicated-left input places the left image in both slots, (Il,Il)(I_{l},I_{l}). Zero-right input replaces the right view with an equally sized black image, (Il,𝟎)(I_{l},\mathbf{0}). Shuffled-right input replaces the correct right image with a right image from another benchmark example, (Il,Ir′)(I_{l},I_{r}^{\prime}). Scores under these four conditions are reported separately and do not enter the primary Stereo3D-Bench score.

Appendix D Additional Results

This section provides the training-data composition and optimization settings omitted from the main paper, followed by geometric generalization evaluation and additional analyses of the single-view capability retained after stereo training, robustness to extrinsic calibration errors, sensitivity to the supplied baseline, and transfer to spatial reasoning and embodied control. We also provide qualitative results and compare modular stereo–VLM pipelines.

D.1 Training Data and Optimization

Stereo training data.

We construct the stereo instruction data from DROID, FSD, Xperience-10M, and RoboCasa. RoboCasa contributes point-level geometry instructions. All stereo pairs are processed using the construction procedure in appendix A.

Table 10 reports the training inventory after filtering and data expansion. Geometry and semantic pairs are counted separately because the two annotation pipelines retain different subsets of the source images. Geometry QA counts denote complete question–answer records rather than individual points within a multi-point question. Semantic counts cover the five object-level task families used in the final model and benchmark.

Geometry-only training data.

The three geometry-only variants compared in table 1 are trained on the same 234K rectified stereo pairs from Xperience-10M, DROID, RoboCasa, and an in-house training collection.

Instruction mixture.

Stereo instructions account for 25%25\% of the final instruction mixture. We allocate 15%15\% to point-level stereo geometry and 10%10\% to object-level stereo semantics, preserving a 60:4060{:}40 ratio within the stereo portion. The remaining 75%75\% is distributed among the monocular and video instruction categories in proportion to their previous weights. The resulting top-level sampling probabilities are shown in table 10. These probabilities specify the composition of the instruction stream after construction of the stereo inventory above.

Optimization.

We initialize each StereoVLM variant from the corresponding Qwen3-VL-Instruct checkpoint and perform full-parameter instruction tuning, including the vision encoder, language model, and multimodal aligner. The final 2B and 8B models share the same training data mixture and optimization schedule. Both are trained for 3,000 optimization steps with an initial learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, a warmup ratio of 0.030.03, and an effective global batch size of 64. We use a maximum sequence length of 32,768 tokens, bfloat16 computation, gradient checkpointing, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-2. Stereo images are presented at 800×320800\times 320, the same resolution used to construct the geometric and semantic references. Dataset and training-order shuffling use a fixed random seed. The reduced-supervision input controls are described separately in section D.6.

D.2 Geometric Generalization to Unseen Scenes

We further evaluate geometric generalization on the in-house OOD split of Stereo3D-Bench. Table 11 reports point-level correspondence, disparity, and depth results using the same metrics as the main split.

D.3 Single-View Capability and Input Controls

Although StereoVLM is trained with explicit stereo supervision, it is not restricted to binocular inputs. Prior work examines how self-supervised monocular depth estimators generalize across domains (Yao et al., 2024). To evaluate the monocular capability retained by the model after stereo instruction tuning, we remove the right image and provide only the rectified left image. We also remove the stereo baseline from the question. The checkpoint, focal length, remaining question text, and decoding configuration are otherwise unchanged. This setting prevents the model from using binocular correspondence and measures what can be recovered from monocular appearance, object-scale priors, and pretrained visual-language knowledge.

Table 12 shows that StereoVLM retains substantial single-view depth and spatial reasoning capability. StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B obtain point-level depth δ1\delta_{1} scores of 73.51 and 63.22, respectively, compared with 43.88 for the strongest general-purpose baseline. StereoVLM-2B also reaches an object-depth δ1\delta_{1} of 81.52. For oriented 3D grounding, StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B achieve mIoU scores of 16.92 and 6.82, respectively. On task-target grounding, their Joint@0.25 scores are 25.64 and 28.21, respectively, exceeding the strongest general-purpose baseline at 7.69.

Compared with the stereo-input results in table 4, GPT-6 Astra’s point-level depth δ1\delta_{1} drops from 75.96% to 43.88%, while its object-depth δ1\delta_{1} falls from 93.40% to 37.37% (table 12). These correspond to decreases of 32.08 and 56.03 percentage points, respectively, indicating substantially higher depth accuracy under the stereo evaluation setting. These results suggest that GPT-6 Astra benefits from stereo conditioning for both point-level and object-level depth estimation, with a more pronounced decline in object-depth accuracy under single-view input.

These results indicate that stereo-representation training does not replace the monocular cues inherited from the pretrained model. Instead, StereoVLM remains usable when only one image is available, while the primary stereo evaluation measures the additional capability obtained from a valid left–right pair. We omit correspondence and disparity from this table because neither quantity is directly observable from a single image.

D.4 Robustness to Extrinsic Calibration Errors

Camera pose determines how 3D scene points project into an image (Yan et al., 2024; Yan and Xu, 2026). We test how sensitive StereoVLM is to small errors in the relative pose of the stereo cameras. Starting from a rectified pair, we keep the left image, query pixels, nominal focal length, nominal baseline, and left-view depth references fixed, and perturb only the pose of the right camera. The resulting right image is rendered under one of six single-axis perturbations: rotations RxR_{x}, RyR_{y}, and RzR_{z}, or translations txt_{x}, tyt_{y}, and tzt_{z}. The experiment therefore measures sensitivity to imperfect stereo alignment without changing the scene or the queried left-view geometry.

The evaluation contains 400 base pairs, comprising 200 DROID pairs and 200 in-house robot pairs. Each pair contributes eight fixed left-image query points. For every axis, we construct three perturbation levels, giving 3,200 queried points per axis and level. The rotation magnitudes are shared across the three rotational axes, and the translation magnitudes are shared across the three translational axes. Averaged over the evaluation set, L1, L2, and L3 correspond to rotations of approximately 0.20∘0.20^{\circ}, 0.59∘0.59^{\circ}, and 0.98∘0.98^{\circ}, or translations of 3.7 mm, 11.1 mm, and 18.4 mm. These magnitudes are selected per pair such that RxR_{x} and tyt_{y} induce mean vertical residuals of approximately 1, 3, and 5 pixels. The other axes use the same physical rotation or translation magnitude rather than being independently adjusted to produce the same image-space displacement.

Figure 9 illustrates the strongest perturbation for each axis. Each row shows the fixed left image, the perturbed right image, and the metric depth produced by FoundationStereo from that pair. The red point in the left image is the queried pixel. In the right image, the green circle marks its nominal correspondence and the red point marks its location after perturbation. The row labels report the mean horizontal and vertical correspondence displacement induced by the perturbation.

Rotations about xx and translations along yy primarily move correspondences away from the original epipolar row. By contrast, RyR_{y} and txt_{x} primarily change horizontal position and therefore alter apparent disparity. The effects of RzR_{z} and tzt_{z} depend on image position and scene depth. FoundationStereo is run on the complete perturbed pair before the common display crop is applied. Its depth maps are included only as a qualitative diagnostic and do not contribute to the StereoVLM results in table 13. Black regions in the translation examples are invalid areas caused by depth-based forward warping.

We evaluate three outputs. Correspondence EPE is measured against the right-image coordinate after perturbation. Direct depth is the metric depth predicted by StereoVLM in response to the depth question. Finally, we derive a depth estimate from the predicted right-image coordinate using

d^i=xil−x^ir,Z^icorr=fx​Bd^i,\hat{d}_{i}=x_{i}^{l}-\hat{x}_{i}^{r},\qquad\hat{Z}_{i}^{\mathrm{corr}}=\frac{f_{x}B}{\hat{d}_{i}}, (15)

where fxf_{x} and BB are the nominal focal length and baseline. Because a perturbed pair does not in general satisfy the nominal rectified-stereo model, this quantity is a diagnostic of prediction under the original calibration rather than a physically corrected triangulation using the perturbed extrinsics. It is derived from the predicted correspondence and is not a separately predicted disparity output.

Table 13 gives the complete results for StereoVLM-2B. Correspondence error increases as the perturbation becomes stronger, from 2.48 pixels without perturbation to 4.93–7.13 pixels under the strongest perturbations. Direct metric depth is more stable. Under rotational perturbations, depth δ1\delta_{1} remains between 90.3% and 91.1%, close to the nominal value of 90.5%. Translation has a larger but still moderate effect: at L3, depth δ1\delta_{1} ranges from 86.1% to 87.8%, and MAE remains below 20 cm.

Depth derived under the nominal calibration follows the same broad trend, decreasing from 90.0% under the nominal condition to 88.0–89.2% under the strongest rotations and 84.6–85.5% under the strongest translations. Meanwhile, correspondence EPE increases consistently with perturbation magnitude. Thus, the model remains numerically stable but does not fully adapt its correspondence predictions to the perturbed geometry. Together with the single-view results in section D.3, this suggests that direct depth combines binocular evidence with monocular and nominal-stereo priors.

D.5 Sensitivity to Baseline Calibration

We evaluate how StereoVLM-2B’s directly generated metric depth answers respond to the baseline specified in the prompt using 400 stereo pairs: 200 from DROID and 200 from our in-house robot dataset. We keep the stereo images, eight query pixels per pair, focal length, and model checkpoint fixed, and replace the nominal baseline B0B_{0} with B=α​B0B=\alpha B_{0}, where α∈{0.6,0.8,0.9,1.0,1.1,1.2,1.5}\alpha\in\{0.6,0.8,0.9,1.0,1.1,1.2,1.5\}.

For each query point ii, we measure the predicted depth ratio

ri​(α)=Z^i​(α​B0)Z^i​(B0).r_{i}(\alpha)=\frac{\hat{Z}_{i}(\alpha B_{0})}{\hat{Z}_{i}(B_{0})}. (16)

With image disparity fixed, the geometric relation Z=fx​B/dZ=f_{x}B/d predicts ideal scaling ri​(α)=αr_{i}(\alpha)=\alpha. This serves as a reference for the model’s directly generated answers. We report the median ratio and its 10th–90th percentile range over all 1,600 query points in each domain, without filtering samples.

As shown in Figure 10, predicted depth increases with the supplied baseline in both domains, with median ratios broadly following the ideal scaling relation. These results suggest that the model uses the supplied baseline for metric depth prediction.

D.6 Additional Transfer Experiments

D.6.1 General Spatial Reasoning

To separate the effects of spatial supervision and binocular input in table 7, we compare three training-input conditions: Correct Stereo uses paired left and right images, Single Left uses only the left image, and Duplicated Left copies the left image into both input positions. All three share a reduced supervision set covering depth estimation, object-level and task-target 3D grounding, and other spatial tasks. Correspondence and disparity questions are excluded from this shared set because Single Left lacks the required right-view observation. StereoVLM uses correctly paired images and additionally includes correspondence and disparity supervision. We evaluate all variants on the same three monocular and two video benchmarks with their standard visual inputs.

Table 14 illustrates the roles of spatial supervision and training input. With the shared supervision set, Correct Stereo, Single Left, and Duplicated Left achieve averages of 50.23, 50.21, and 49.46, respectively, all exceeding the 47.94 baseline without stereo instruction tuning. Additional spatial supervision therefore benefits transfer even without valid stereo pairs. Correct Stereo improves over Duplicated Left by 0.77 points, but performs similarly to Single Left on average, indicating that paired images alone do not ensure stronger transfer.

With full geometric supervision, StereoVLM achieves the highest average of 51.48, exceeding Correct Stereo by 1.25 points, and leads on both MindCube and VSI-Bench. Although no configuration dominates every benchmark, these results support combining correspondence, disparity, and depth supervision to improve overall spatial-reasoning transfer.

D.6.2 Embodied Control

Transfer of geometric supervision. We evaluate the configurations in section D.6.1 on downstream manipulation, using the same visual input configuration during training and evaluation. When point-level geometric supervision is limited to depth, the correct-stereo and single-left configurations achieve similar success rates (38.2% and 37.7%; table 15). Within the correct-stereo configuration, adding correspondence and disparity supervision raises success to 42.4%, a gain of 4.2 percentage points. This improvement supports explicitly supervising cross-view geometry when learning representations for embodied control.

Dependence on binocular observations. We further examine whether stereo representation learning transfers to embodied control. For each VLM initialization, we train separate stereo and single-left policies under the same downstream training protocol. The stereo policy is evaluated with either the correct stereo pair or the left image duplicated into the right-view slot; these two results use the same policy checkpoint. The single-left policy is trained and evaluated using only the left image. Table 16 reports average task success rates.

Without stereo representation training, the separately trained single-left policies outperform their stereo counterparts: 36.4% versus 34.9% for Qwen3-VL, and 39.5% versus 38.1% for StereoVLM-2B w/o Stereo Supervision. Thus, adding a right view does not by itself improve control under this training protocol.

With stereo representation training, the stereo policy reaches 42.4% success, the highest result in the table. This exceeds the separately trained single-left policy initialized from the same VLM by 2.4 percentage points. Because the policies are trained separately, this comparison measures the outcome of two training configurations, not the effect of removing the right view at inference time.

For the stereo-trained policy, replacing the right image with a copy of the left reduces success from 42.4% to 26.3%. This 16.1-point drop is a within-checkpoint intervention: it preserves the two-image input format while removing the valid stereo pairing. The result shows that this policy is sensitive to the content of the right-view slot, although the intervention alone cannot distinguish geometric dependence from other effects of an out-of-distribution input.

D.7 Qualitative Visual Results

Figure 11 compares dense depth predictions across DROID, Xperience-10M, and the in-house OOD split. Alongside the standard stereo-input result, we show the same StereoVLM-2B checkpoint with monocular input and the DepthVLM-4B baseline for reference.

Figure 12 visualizes representative semantic predictions under the standard stereo-input condition. Although only the rectified left image is shown for readability, both models receive the complete rectified left–right pair when producing each prediction. The three row groups correspond to object metric depth, semantic oriented 3D grounding, and task-target grounding.

For object depth, the yellow 2D box identifies the referred object and the label reports its predicted optical-axis depth in meters. For semantic 3D grounding, each oriented 3D box is projected into the rectified-left image. Task-target grounding additionally requires the model to identify the visible object specified by the manipulation instruction before predicting its 3D box. Green marks the reference; orange and blue mark StereoVLM-2B and StereoVLM-8B predictions, respectively.

In these examples, both model scales recover object depth closely and produce 3D boxes with similar centers, extents, and orientations to the references. The task-target examples further illustrate that the models can connect a manipulation instruction to the appropriate scene object and localize it in 3D. These examples are qualitative illustrations; aggregate performance and controlled input comparisons are reported in the main experiments.

D.8 Comparison with Modular Stereo–VLM Pipelines

We evaluate whether a general-purpose VLM equipped with an external stereo estimator can achieve comparable object-level spatial reasoning to StereoVLM. We construct two modular baselines using FoundationStereo (Wen et al., 2025) and a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), and compare their semantic accuracy and end-to-end inference latency with StereoVLM-2B.

Baseline construction.

The two baselines differ in how stereo geometry is provided to the VLM. The localization-based pipeline first queries the VLM to localize the referred object in the left image. It then aggregates FoundationStereo-predicted disparities within the localized region using a fixed central-window median and disparity-based filtering. The selected pixels are back-projected into 3D, and a PCA-based heuristic estimates an approximate oriented bounding box of the visible surface. These geometric measurements are then provided to the VLM to generate the final answer. The direct-input pipeline instead provides the stereo RGB pair, a predicted depth visualization, an 8×208\times 20 disparity/depth grid, and camera calibration to the VLM in a single call. Neither baseline receives ground-truth answers, bounding boxes, or masks at inference time. StereoVLM-2B directly answers each question from the stereo RGB pair and the task prompt, including the applicable camera calibration, in one VLM call.

Accuracy and efficiency.

Compared with modular pipelines that explicitly estimate geometry and pass it to a frozen VLM, StereoVLM predicts language-referred object geometry and task targets directly from stereo images in a single VLM call. This removes the separate stereo estimator and intermediate region-pooling or geometry-encoding stages. As shown in table 17, StereoVLM-2B achieves higher accuracy on all five semantic tasks and lower end-to-end latency in this comparison, with 3.44×3.44\times and 1.43×1.43\times speedups over the localization-based and direct-input pipelines, respectively.
